domains.name: Billing
domains.summary: Charging guests for their stays, and getting paid.
domains.body:
A booking here is what a guest is charged for a stay, not the hold on a room
that Guest stays means by it.

domains.name: Finance
domains.summary: Keeping the hotel's accounts, and getting paid by the companies it bills.

features.name: Guest bills
features.summary: Keeping an accurate record of what each guest owes during their stay.

features.name: Payments
features.summary: Getting paid for stays, before the guest arrives and while they're here.

features.name: Company accounts
features.summary: Billing companies for their staff's stays, so the guests don't pay themselves.

features.name: Closing the day
features.summary: Making each day's takings final, and handing them to the hotel's accounts.

features.name: Front desk
features.summary: Welcoming guests when they arrive and settling up when they leave.
features.body:
Billing's part of the front desk is settling the bill at check-out. Checking
guests in and out is Guest stays'.

personas.name: Priya, bookkeeper
personas.summary: Keeps the hotel's books, and invoices the companies that pay for their staff's stays.
personas.body:
## Needs

- To get each day's takings into the accounting software without typing them
  in.
- To invoice every company once a month, and see what each one owes.
- To keep companies within the credit the hotel allows them.

## Knows

Bookkeeping, and the hotel's accounting software, well. Less about how the
front desk works.

## Context

Part time, two or three days a week, at a desk in the back office. Month end
is their busiest time.

## Expects

Days that are closed and stay closed, invoice numbers that run in order, and
an export their accounting software takes as it is.

## Cares about

Books that balance. A day that changes after they've exported it means finding
the difference by hand.

personas.name: Maria, front desk clerk
personas.summary: Runs the front desk: takes bookings, and checks guests in and out.
personas.body:
## Needs

- To see everything a guest owes on one bill, so check-out is a single
  payment.
- To put extras on a bill the moment they happen, so nothing is forgotten.
- To let company guests leave without paying, knowing their company will be
  invoiced.

## Knows

What every extra costs, and which guests' companies pay for their stays. Not
an accountant: they think in bills, not ledgers.

## Context

At the desk, with the guest in front of them and often a queue behind. Check-out
mornings are the busiest part of their day.

## Expects

A bill that reads like a receipt: each night, each extra, then the total.
Payments by card at the desk.

## Cares about

A bill the guest doesn't argue with. A charge they can't explain, or one they
can't take off when it was a mistake, makes for a hard conversation.

personas.name: Sam, guest
personas.summary: Stays at the hotel, for work or on holiday, and pays for the stay.
personas.body:
## Needs

- To pay without queueing at the desk on the way out.
- To leave without paying when their company is paying for the stay.
- A bill they can understand, with nothing on it they didn't have.

## Knows

Nothing about the hotel's systems. Pays for things online and by card all the
time.

## Context

On their phone, often in a hurry: packing, catching a train, or already home.

## Expects

Paying by link to work like any other online payment, in a minute or two.

## Cares about

Not being charged twice, and not being chased for something they've paid.

personas.name: David, hotel manager
personas.summary: Runs the hotel, and answers for its takings to the owners.
personas.body:
## Needs

- To see each day's takings, final and broken down, without waiting for the
  bookkeeper.
- To be sure every night, every extra and the city's tax are charged, so the
  hotel isn't out of pocket.
- To be covered when a guest who booked never arrives.

## Knows

The hotel's numbers: occupancy, the average rate, last year's takings.
Not the details of how the books are kept.

## Context

Looks at the numbers first thing each morning, on a laptop or their phone.

## Expects

Totals for rooms, food and drink, and tax, the way the owners ask for them.

## Cares about

Numbers that don't change once a day is closed. If yesterday's takings move,
they stop trusting all of them.

personas.name: Tom, night auditor
personas.summary: Looks after the hotel overnight, and makes sure each day is closed before morning.
personas.body:
## Needs

- To know the day was closed and every guest charged for the night, without
  staying up to do it by hand.
- To close the day themselves when the audit didn't run on its own.

## Knows

The night audit's steps, from years of doing them on paper. Less at ease with
software that does them for them.

## Context

At the front desk overnight, alone, with few guests around and no one to ask.

## Expects

To see, at a glance, that tonight's audit has run, and what it charged.

## Cares about

Not handing over to the morning shift with yesterday still open.

capabilities.name: Extra charges
capabilities.summary: Staff add extras such as breakfast, parking or the minibar to a guest's bill.
capabilities.body:
## Covers

- Clerks correct a charge that was added by mistake.

## Success

- No guest leaves with an extra that never reached their bill.

capabilities.name: City tax
capabilities.summary: The software adds the city's tourist tax to each guest's bill, night by night.
capabilities.body:
## Covers

- Clerks see the city tax on a guest's bill, night by night.

capabilities.name: Split bills
capabilities.summary: Clerks split a bill between guests sharing a room, or move charges onto another guest's bill.
capabilities.body:
## Learning

- Do guests split evenly, or charge by charge?

capabilities.name: Deposits
capabilities.summary: The software takes a deposit on the guest's card when a stay is booked.
capabilities.body:
## Covers

- Clerks see whether a stay's deposit has been paid.
- Clerks take a deposit again when the guest's card was declined.

## Open decisions

- **Long stays:** is a week's stay still secured by one night's deposit?

capabilities.name: Pay by link
capabilities.summary: Guests pay their bill by card from a link the hotel sends them, without coming to the desk.
capabilities.body:
## Covers

- Clerks send a guest a link to pay what they owe.

## Learning

- Do guests pay before they leave, or wait until they're home?

capabilities.name: Company accounts
capabilities.summary: Bookkeepers set up companies that pay for their staff's stays, each with a credit limit.
capabilities.body:
## Covers

- Bookkeepers name the guests whose stays a company pays for.
- Bookkeepers see what each company owes.

capabilities.name: Direct billing
capabilities.summary: Clerks move a guest's bill to their company's account at check-out, so the guest leaves without paying.

capabilities.name: Invoices
capabilities.summary: Bookkeepers invoice each company once a month for its staff's stays.
capabilities.body:
## Covers

- Bookkeepers record a company's payment against its invoice.

capabilities.name: Night audit
capabilities.summary: The software closes each business day overnight, charging every guest in the hotel for that night's room.
capabilities.body:
## Covers

- Night auditors see whether tonight's audit has run, and what it charged.
- Night auditors start the audit by hand when it hasn't run.

## Success

- Every morning starts with yesterday closed, without anyone staying up for it.

capabilities.name: Daily takings
capabilities.summary: Managers see each closed day's takings, for rooms, food and drink, and tax.
capabilities.body:
## Covers

- Managers compare a day with the same day last year.

capabilities.name: Accounting export
capabilities.summary: Bookkeepers export each closed day's takings to the hotel's accounting software.
capabilities.body:
## Learning

- Is a day at a time what the accountant wants, or one export a month?

capabilities.name: Check-out
capabilities.summary: Guests settle their bill as they leave, so nothing is left owing once they've gone.
capabilities.body:
## Covers

- Clerks see a departing guest's bill, with every night and charge on it.
- Clerks take payment for the balance, and close the bill.

## Learning

- Do guests want their bill emailed as they leave, or printed at the desk?

rules.name: A charge is never changed or deleted
rules.summary: A charge is corrected by adding a charge for the opposite amount, never by changing or deleting it.

verifiedBy.test: A charge is never changed or deleted

rules.body:
## Why

The hotel's accountant and the tax office need to see every charge that was
made, including the mistakes.

rules.name: A closed bill can't change
rules.summary: Nothing can be charged or paid on a closed bill. A charge that arrives after the guest has left goes on a new bill for the same stay.

verifiedBy.test: post > refuses a charge on a closed bill

rules.name: City tax is charged per guest, per night
rules.summary: Each guest on a stay is charged the city's tax for each night, at the rate on that night.

verifiedBy.test: City tax is charged per guest, per night

rules.body:
## Why

The hotel owes the city tax for every guest night, whether or not it charged
the guest.

rules.name: Children pay no city tax
rules.summary: Guests under 16 aren't charged city tax.

rules.name: City tax stops after seven nights
rules.summary: A guest staying longer than seven nights is charged city tax for the first seven only.

rules.name: Moving charges keeps the total
rules.summary: Splitting a bill or moving charges between bills never changes the total owed across them.

rules.name: A deposit is the first night
rules.summary: A stay's deposit is the first night's room rate, with its city tax.

verifiedBy.test: A deposit is the first night

rules.name: A deposit counts towards the bill
rules.summary: A deposit is a payment on the guest's bill, so the guest pays only the rest at check-out.

verifiedBy.test: applyDeposit > counts the deposit towards the bill

rules.name: Card numbers are never kept
rules.summary: The hotel never stores a guest's card number. Only the payment provider holds it.
rules.body:
## Why

Holding card numbers would put the hotel under the card schemes' security
audits.

rules.name: A company can't go over its credit limit
rules.summary: A bill can't move to a company's account if it would take what the company owes over its credit limit.

verifiedBy.test: A company can't go over its credit limit

rules.name: Only named guests' bills go to a company
rules.summary: A bill can move to a company's account only if the company has named the guest as someone whose stays it pays for.

rules.name: Invoice numbers run in sequence
rules.summary: Each invoice's number is one more than the last, with none skipped or used twice.

verifiedBy.test: nextInvoiceNumber > follows the last invoice's number

rules.body:
## Why

The tax office requires it, so it can tell no invoice is missing.

rules.name: A guest is charged once a night for their room
rules.summary: Each guest in the hotel is charged for their room once for each night, even if the audit is started more than once.

verifiedBy.test: A guest is charged once a night for their room

rules.name: A closed day can't change
rules.summary: Once a business day is closed, nothing is added to it. A correction to a closed day goes on the current one.
rules.body:
## Why

A closed day's takings have already gone to the accountant.

rules.name: Overpayments are refunded
rules.summary: A guest who has paid more than their bill is refunded the difference before the bill closes.

concepts.name: Bill
concepts.summary: Everything a guest owes for one stay, and everything they've paid towards it.
concepts.body:
## Details

A bill is made of [charges](charge.md) and [payments](payment.md). Its balance
is what's been charged less what's been paid. A guest's bill can move to their
[company's account](company-account.md), which then owes it instead.

## Lifecycle

Open → Closed

A bill closes when its balance is zero, or when it moves to a company's
account.

## Not to be confused with

- **Invoice:** what a company is sent for a month of its staff's bills.

concepts.name: Business day
concepts.summary: The hotel's day for its accounts, from one night audit to the next.
concepts.body:
## Details

A business day isn't a calendar day. It runs from when one night audit closes
the day before, usually around 03:00, until the next audit closes it. A
breakfast at 02:00 is on the previous business day.

## Lifecycle

Open → Closed

concepts.name: Charge
concepts.summary: One amount a guest owes, such as a night's room, a breakfast or a night's city tax.
concepts.body:
## Details

Each charge is on one [bill](bill.md), and on the
[business day](business-day.md) it was added. A correction is a charge for the
opposite amount, pointing at the charge it corrects.

concepts.name: Company account
concepts.summary: A company that pays for its staff's stays, and what it owes the hotel.
concepts.body:
## Details

A company account has a credit limit, and names the guests whose
[bills](bill.md) it pays. It's invoiced once a month for the bills moved to it.

concepts.name: Payment
concepts.summary: Money a guest has paid towards their bill, by card or in cash.
concepts.body:
## Details

A deposit is a payment taken before the guest arrives. A card payment is
known by the provider's reference, never by the card's number.

## Lifecycle

Pending → Paid

A pending card payment can instead be Declined.

concepts.name: Booking
concepts.summary: What a guest is charged for a stay: its nights, at the rate agreed when it was booked.
concepts.body:
## Details

A booking puts one room charge per night on the guest's [bill](bill.md), at its
agreed rate, whatever the rate is on the night.

## Not to be confused with

- **The booking app's booking:** a guest's hold on a room. Billing doesn't
  keep rooms free or taken, only what each stay costs.

gaps.text: Guests' ages aren't recorded, so city tax is added for every guest on a stay, and clerks correct it by hand for children.
Guests pay in the hotel's currency. Their card provider converts it, at its own rate.
A bill moves to a company's account whole. A guest who pays for their own extras pays for them before their bill moves.
Nothing reminds a company when an invoice is overdue. The bookkeeper checks the unpaid invoices each week and chases them by email.

areas.name: Direction and feedback
areas.why: We're building the right thing, and we know it.

items.text: What it's for is written down: the question it answers, or the problem it solves.
The client can reach it, try it, and react to it.
The client's feedback is recorded, and shapes what comes next.
Hooked up end to end. Sample data is fine if the system itself stores and serves it.
People who'd want to try it can find out it exists and how to opt in.
Feedback comes from real use, not just demos.
The client agrees its shape has settled.
What success looks like is agreed with the client.
Shown to meet that success in real use.

areas.name: Tests
areas.why: What's been checked, and what keeps it from breaking again.

items.text: The main path works when someone tries it by hand.
The main path is checked automatically (such as unit, integration, or end-to-end tests).
Checks run on every change, and a failure stops it from shipping (such as CI that blocks merging).
Edge cases and error paths are checked.
Critical workflows checked end to end.
Every fixed bug has a check that would catch it coming back.
Checks can be trusted: none flaky or skipped without being tracked.

areas.name: Edge cases and errors
areas.why: What happens with unusual input, and when something goes wrong.

items.text: Errors fail visibly, never silently.
Input validated where it enters.
Empty, missing, duplicate, and large inputs handled.
Error messages say what went wrong and what to do next, without exposing internals.
Concurrent use and partial failures handled (two at once, a crash halfway through), and repeating an operation is safe.
Every known edge case handled or documented as out of scope.

areas.name: Data and migrations
areas.why: Your data stays correct, and can be recovered if something goes wrong.

items.text: Sample data is clearly marked wherever it appears.
Data it creates can be cleaned up.
Data people put in is kept across changes.
Changes to the shape of stored data apply the same way everywhere, without hand edits (such as migration scripts).
Data validated before it's written.
A data change that goes wrong can be undone (such as a reversible migration, or a backup taken first).
Data changes tried on production-sized data before they ship.
Stored data can be recovered after a loss, and recovery has been tried (such as backups with a tested restore).

areas.name: Performance and cost
areas.why: It's fast enough for the work, today and at peak, at a cost that makes sense.

items.text: Responsive enough for the people trying it.
Usable with today's real amounts of data and use.
Tried at realistic volumes, with bounded work (queries, memory, input size).
Obvious problems fixed (such as a query or call per item, missing indexes, loading everything into memory, slow startup).
Meets performance targets agreed with the client, measured (such as response time, throughput, or startup time).
Handles peak load, or the largest expected input, with headroom.
What it costs to run is known, and fits expected use.

areas.name: Security, privacy, and compliance
areas.why: Your systems and data are protected the same way at every level, and the work follows the rules that apply to it.

items.text: Secrets kept out of code, version control, sample data, and demos (such as in the secret store).
Secrets and personal data kept out of logs, error messages, and output.
Real client data comes only through production systems, never copied into code, sample data, or fixtures.
Access control enforced on anything touching client systems or data.
People can only see and change data they're allowed to. One client or customer can never see or change another's.
Personal data collected only where needed.
Untrusted input can't run as code or commands (such as SQL injection or cross-site scripting).
Personal data can be exported and deleted on request.
Protected against misuse at the level it's exposed to (such as rate limits, abuse of sign-ups, or scraping).
The legal and regulatory duties that apply are known (such as privacy law, industry rules, where data may be stored, and contracts).
Reviewed for security wherever it handles credentials, payments, personal data, or permissions.
Each part has only the access it needs, and sensitive actions can be traced to who did them.
Stored data kept only as long as it's needed.
The legal and regulatory duties that apply are met.

areas.name: Dependencies and integrations
areas.why: What it relies on, and what happens when those things change or fail.

items.text: Depends on nothing less stable than itself (for a third party, a release at a matching stage).
Dependencies maintained, with compatible licenses.
Settings that differ between environments kept out of code (such as service URLs and keys).
Builds use the same dependency versions every time, and known vulnerabilities in them are found.
When an external service is slow or down, it fails clearly instead of hanging (such as timeouts, and retries where safe).
The rate limits and quotas of what it depends on fit expected use.
Dependencies kept current (such as automated or scheduled updates).

areas.name: Logs, traces, and metrics
areas.why: When something goes wrong, we can see what happened and why.

items.text: Errors logged with context.
Whoever operates it can read the logs.
Everything from one request, job, or run can be found together (such as structured logs with a shared ID).
Whoever operates it hears about errors without searching the logs (such as an error tracker).
How often key operations run and fail, and how long they take, is measured.
Whether the main workflows succeed is measured, not just whether the system is up.
A failed critical workflow can be followed from start to finish (such as traces linked from logs).
Logs are kept no longer than privacy needs allow.

areas.name: Monitoring and alerting
areas.why: Whoever operates it finds out something is wrong before your users do.

items.text: Health checked automatically (such as uptime checks for services, or success checks for scheduled jobs).
Key metrics visible at a glance (such as a dashboard).
Targets set and tracked for latency, error rate, and availability.
Whoever operates production is alerted to failures users would notice.
Every alert says what to do about it (such as a linked runbook).
Alerts are known to fire, and quiet enough that people act on them.

areas.name: Release and rollback
areas.why: How it reaches your users, and how quickly it can be undone.

items.text: Its stability level is clear wherever people see it (a stability mark, or no mark once it's GA).
Not available to users by default (such as outside production, or behind a flag that's off).
Can be removed cleanly, and can't affect anything people rely on, including production data.
Opt-in only (such as only for invited users, or behind a feature flag).
Released the same way as the rest of the product (such as the normal deploy pipeline).
Can be rolled back to the previous version.
Rollback has been tried.
It can be set up again from scratch without hand steps, such as after losing its environment.
For software others install, users can verify a release came from us (such as signed builds).

areas.name: Ownership and support
areas.why: Someone is responsible for it, and you know what happens when it breaks.

items.text: It has an owner who decides what happens to it.
Bugs recorded where the team tracks its work.
The client and users know how to report a problem.
Bugs triaged and fixed as found.
Known bugs shared with the client.
GA bugs fixed before new work.
The client and users know where to get help, and what response to expect.
The owner is responsible for keeping it running long term, including who responds outside working hours, if it's critical enough to need that.
During a serious outage, users can find out what's happening (such as a status page or an announcement).
Serious incidents are reviewed so they're less likely to happen again.

areas.name: User experience
areas.why: The people using it can get their work done, without surprises.

items.text: Its main idea is clear to the people using it.
A real user can complete the main workflow.
Waiting, empty, and error states handled on purpose (such as loading, no results, and clear error messages).
Usable by everyone it's meant for, the way they use it (such as keyboard access, labels, and contrast in a UI, or help text in a command-line tool).
Supported platforms, languages, and regions listed (such as browsers, devices, and time zones), and it works the same on each.
Meets the project's accessibility standard.

areas.name: Documentation
areas.why: You, your users, and the next engineer can use, run, and change it without asking the author.

items.text: What it does, and what it doesn't handle yet, is written down where the client can see it.
Developers: how to run it.
Users: how to try it.
Developers: its configuration.
Users: how to use and configure it.
Developers: how it's put together, and the key decisions behind it.
Users told what changed in each release (such as release notes or a changelog).
Users: complete, current documentation.
Developers: reference docs for its public interface.
Operations: how to deploy, roll back, and diagnose it, or for software others install, how to install, upgrade, and troubleshoot it.

areas.name: Code and maintainability
areas.why: It can keep changing, by any engineer, without getting harder to change.

items.text: Follows the project's conventions, and passes its automated checks (such as lint and type checks).
Reviewed by another engineer, where the team has one.
Earlier shortcuts removed or tracked.
Another engineer can change it without the author.
No untracked TODOs or dead code.

areas.name: Breaking changes
areas.why: What you build on it keeps working, or you hear first.

items.text: What's part of its public interface, and what's internal, is clear.
People building on it have somewhere to hear about changes (such as release notes or a changelog).
Breaking changes kept to a minimum, and announced ahead of time where we can, with how to move to the new behavior.
Public interfaces documented as stable.
Breaking changes announced ahead of time, with a deprecation window long enough to move (such as a new version, with the previous one kept working for a set time).
